endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: CHAI recommends collecting this information through a model card (see CHAI’s Applied Model Card, hereafter “Applied Model Card AMC)”) or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire

commentary.bottom_line: One voluntary framework, the CHAI governance playbooks, supports collecting AI solution information through a model card and a standardized intake questionnaire, but no study has tested a tiered intake that pairs a brief screener with a longer questionnaire for medium- and high-risk tools. Health systems that adopt this practice are relying on expert consensus rather than measured effects on review capacity or missed risks.

perspectives.view: No study tests tiered intake, and no study documents the target hazard of overwhelmed review capacity or missed high-risk details. The only support is one framework statement. Under GRADE conventions, this leaves no direct evidence on whether the practice changes review throughput, accuracy of risk classification, or downstream harm.

The CHAI endorsement recommends a model card or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire. The quoted text does not itself specify risk tiers or a two-step screener. Health systems should treat the tiered design as a local extension of voluntary guidance rather than as a requirement of any regulation.

A triage screener introduces a single decision point where a high-risk tool could be classified as low risk and receive only light review. No study measures how often this misclassification occurs or whether the longer questionnaire detects problems that the screener misses.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tiered intake with uniform intake across governance committees and that measure review time, backlog, the rate at which the screener assigns tools to the wrong risk tier, and the number of safety or bias issues found before deployment.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether screener questions would flag risks specific to these groups, such as language access or performance in under-resourced settings, and safety-net systems with small governance staff may face different capacity trade-offs.
